definition: A way for one machine's network card to read or write another machine's memory directly, without either operating system copying the data. It cuts latency and CPU work, which is why AI clusters use it for GPU-to-GPU traffic.

RDMA carried inside Ethernet packets (RoCEv2 uses UDP/IP). It brings InfiniBand-style direct memory transfers to Ethernet, but needs careful congestion control because Ethernet was designed to drop packets when busy.

The delay of the slowest messages (for example the 99th or 99.9th percentile), not the average. In synchronous AI training the whole step waits for the slowest transfer, so the tail, not the mean, sets the pace.
A GPU, link or flow that finishes late and makes every other participant in a synchronous step wait. Causes include congested paths, slow or failing hardware and uneven work.

Many senders transmitting to one receiver at the same moment, overflowing the switch port in front of it. Collective operations create incast by design, which is why AI fabrics need congestion control.

The rules senders and switches use to slow traffic before queues overflow, for example by marking packets (ECN) and having NICs cut their sending rate. Good congestion control keeps queues short and tail latency low.

An Ethernet mechanism that tells the upstream device to pause a traffic class when a buffer fills, so packets are not dropped. It makes Ethernet 'lossless' for RoCE but can spread pauses through the fabric if overused.
A bit a switch sets in packets when its queue starts to fill. The receiver echoes it back and the sender slows down, preventing drops without pausing the link.
Standard Ethernet load balancing that hashes each flow onto one of several equal-length paths. Large AI flows can collide on the same path while others sit idle, wasting bandwidth.

Choosing the path for each packet (or group of packets) based on live queue depths instead of a fixed hash, steering traffic around hot spots. InfiniBand has it natively; Spectrum-X and Ultra Ethernet add it to Ethernet.
Spreading the packets of a single flow across many paths at once. It uses the whole fabric evenly but packets arrive out of order, so the receiving NIC must put them back in sequence.

InfiniBand's way of avoiding drops: a sender may only transmit when the receiver has advertised free buffer space ('credits'). Nothing is sent that cannot be stored, so the link is lossless by construction.

The InfiniBand control software that discovers every switch and adapter, assigns addresses and computes the routing tables for the whole fabric. It makes InfiniBand centrally managed rather than self-organizing like Ethernet.

NVIDIA's Scalable Hierarchical Aggregation and Reduction Protocol: switches add up the data from many GPUs as it passes through, so each GPU sends its data once instead of about twice during an all-reduce. Available in Quantum InfiniBand and NVLink switches.
Doing simple computation, such as summing gradients, inside the network switches instead of on the endpoints. It cuts the data that crosses the network and frees GPU time.

A multi-tier switch topology in which links get 'fatter' toward the top so that any endpoint can talk to any other at full speed. With switches of radix R, two tiers connect R²/2 endpoints and three tiers R³/4.

A cluster wiring pattern in which NIC number k of every server connects to the same 'rail' leaf switch, so same-numbered GPUs across servers are one switch hop apart. It matches how collective libraries move data.
The number of ports on a switch at a given speed. Higher radix means more endpoints per tier, fewer tiers, fewer hops and fewer optics for the same cluster.

The total bandwidth across the narrowest cut that splits the network into two equal halves. A non-blocking fat tree has full bisection bandwidth: half the endpoints can talk to the other half at line rate.
Having more downlink than uplink bandwidth at a switch tier (for example 3:1), which saves switches and optics but means not every endpoint can send across the tier at full speed at once.
Traffic between servers inside a data center (for example GPU-to-GPU gradient exchange), as opposed to traffic entering or leaving it. AI training is dominated by east-west traffic.
Traffic between a data center and the outside world: users, the internet and other sites.
The dedicated GPU-to-GPU fabric (InfiniBand or AI Ethernet) used for training and large-scale inference collectives, separate from the general-purpose network.
The conventional data-center network that connects servers to storage, users, management systems and the internet.
NVIDIA's name for a network adapter tuned for GPU-to-GPU traffic (ConnectX-8/9, BlueField-3 SuperNIC): RDMA, congestion control and reordering of sprayed packets in hardware, typically one per GPU.
An NVIDIA feature that lets the network card read and write GPU memory directly, skipping a copy through CPU memory.

Placing the optical engines that turn electrical signals into light right next to the switch chip on the same package, instead of in pluggable modules at the front panel. It shortens the electrical path and cuts power per bit.

A removable optical module (for example an 800G or 1.6T OSFP) that plugs into a switch or NIC port and converts electrical signals to light. Easy to replace, but it needs a power-hungry DSP to drive signals across the circuit board.
Serializer/deserializer: the circuit that turns many parallel on-chip signals into a few very fast serial lanes (today 100–200 Gb/s each) and back. Port speed = lanes × lane rate.

A tiny ring-shaped silicon-photonics device that switches light on and off to encode data. Very small and low-power, it is the modulator NVIDIA uses in its CPO engines (built on TSMC's COUPE process), but it is sensitive to temperature.

In CPO designs, the lasers sit in separate replaceable modules on the front panel and feed light to the optical engines by fiber, because lasers are the part most likely to fail and dislike the heat next to a switch chip.
A pluggable module without its own DSP chip, relying on the switch's SerDes to drive the signal. Roughly halves module power but shortens reach and tightens interoperability.
NVIDIA's 2025 extension of Spectrum-X Ethernet for 'scale-across': algorithms for distance-aware congestion control and latency management that let GPU fabrics in different data centers act as one.

An industry specification from the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (version 1.0 in June 2025) that adds AI-oriented transport, packet spraying, congestion control and other features to standard Ethernet, so any vendor's NICs and switches can match proprietary AI fabrics.

A fabric built as several independent parallel networks ('planes'), with each GPU's NIC split across them. Lower-radix ports per plane let two tiers reach more GPUs, and a failed plane only removes part of the bandwidth.
